macro: August's CPI report, released Friday, showed headline inflation at 3.4% year-over-year (+0.4% month-over-month) and core CPI at 2.4% year-over-year (+0.3% month-over-month, a tenth above forecast), reinforcing the view that inflation is not cleanly returning to the Fed's 2% target. The report pushed CME FedWatch odds of a quarter-point hike at the September 16 FOMC meeting to nearly 87%, up from about 72% just before the release and from roughly 48% a month ago, as new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole remarks continue to reshape expectations. Stocks and bonds both rallied Friday anyway, as a sharp pullback in oil prices offset the hotter inflation print. The single most important event this week is Wednesday, September 16, when the FOMC announces its rate decision at 2:00pm ET, followed by Chair Warsh's press conference.

energy: WTI crude fell 2.53% to $99.99 a barrel, pulling back after Brent paused its rally to settle near $104 on Friday, September 11. The EIA's most recent report showed commercial crude inventories fell just 0.4 million barrels in the week ended September 4, a smaller draw than the 1.55-million-barrel decline analysts had expected. The Strait of Hormuz disruption remains the dominant supply risk, but Friday's pullback suggests some traders are starting to fade the geopolitical premium even as the underlying risk hasn't changed.
vix_and_dollar: The VIX closed at 15.84 on September 11, down 11.2% from the prior session's 17.89 and back in the 'normal' 15-20 band after a brief spike. The Dollar Index held above 99 at 99.11, little changed on the day even as the CPI report cemented near-90% odds of a Fed rate hike — a combination suggesting markets are treating the hike as a known quantity rather than a fresh risk-off trigger.
mortgage_rate: The 30-year fixed mortgage rate is holding at 6.76% in Freddie Mac's Primary Mortgage Market Survey for the week of September 10, 2026, its most recent published reading, up from 6.71% two weeks earlier. Existing-home sales fell 2% in August to 3.98 million annualized units even as inventory rose to a decade-high 4.9 months of supply, underscoring that elevated rates, not a lack of listings, remain the binding constraint on affordability.
personal_finance_deep_dive: Average hourly earnings rose just 3.1% year-over-year in August, the slowest pace in more than five years, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Employment Situation report released September 4, 2026. Wage growth has been decelerating for six straight months, down from 3.7% in February, even as headline inflation has run at or above 3.4% for most of the year, meaning real, inflation-adjusted pay has been flat to negative for large stretches of 2026. Hourly and lower-wage workers are most exposed, since their pay tracks nominal wage indices most closely and they carry the least cushion when a paycheck's real value stalls. Decelerating pay growth is also typically an early signal that labor demand itself is cooling, not just that inflation is easing.
wealth_building_deep_dive: US-listed ETFs are on pace to pull in a record $2.3 trillion in 2026, comfortably eclipsing 2025's $1.5 trillion record, after collecting roughly $180 billion in August alone despite that month's usual seasonal slowdown, according to State Street Investment Management. The flows are overwhelmingly passive: index funds and ETFs now hold more combined assets than actively managed funds, a structural shift that keeps rewarding low-cost, broad-market exposure over stock-picking. The practical takeaway isn't to chase the flows into any single fund, but to check this week whether new retirement or brokerage contributions are still defaulting into a low-cost, broad-market index fund rather than sitting in cash or an actively managed fund whose fee has to be overcome before it adds any value.
